title: Danus: Orchestrating Mathematical Reasoning Agents with Fact-Graph Memory
hook: Parallel proof-search agents can generate claims faster than anyone can keep straight. Danus fixes that with a shared fact graph that only admits claims a stateless verifier has checked.
key_points: Danus splits math reasoning into a main planning agent plus multiple parallel worker agents doing proof search.
A stateless verifier checks every proposed claim before it enters a shared 'fact graph' with its proof and dependencies.
The main agent periodically summarizes the proof state, redirects workers, and reports progress to a human mathematician.
Evaluated on six research-level case studies in algebraic geometry, singularity theory, and combinatorics.
Fact-graph memory lets Danus build long, detailed proofs incrementally instead of losing coherence across many steps.
content_html: Scaling math reasoning agents past textbook problems means coordinating many parallel provers without losing track of what's actually been proven. Danus tackles that coordination problem with a shared fact graph that only admits claims a stateless verifier has checked.
extra_html:
How it's built

Danus splits work between a main agent that plans, coordinates, and periodically summarizes progress, and multiple worker agents that search for proofs in parallel. Every claim a worker proposes passes through a stateless verifier before it's stored in the shared fact graph alongside its proof and logical dependencies — so partial results accumulate into a reliable, growing base the whole team can build on, and the main agent can redirect workers or report progress to a human mathematician.

Why it matters

The authors test Danus on six research-level case studies spanning algebraic geometry, singularity theory, and combinatorics, showing the fact-graph mechanism lets it construct long, detailed proofs rather than losing coherence over many steps. It's a system-design answer to a specific failure mode: multi-agent proof search generating claims faster than anyone, human or model, can verify and keep organized. Danus is open source. Liu, Gao, and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

flashcards.prompt: What problem does Danus's fact-graph memory solve for multi-agent math reasoning?
flashcards.back_html: Parallel proof-search workers can generate claims faster than they can be checked and organized. The fact graph only admits claims a stateless verifier has confirmed, keeping the shared proof state reliable as it grows.

flashcards.prompt: What are the three components in Danus's architecture?

choices.text: A main planning/coordinating agent, multiple parallel worker agents doing proof search, and a stateless verifier gating the shared fact graph
A single agent that both proposes and verifies every claim itself
A human mathematician who manually verifies every step

flashcards.explanation_html: Danus separates coordination (main agent), parallel search (workers), and gating (verifier) so no single component both proposes and blesses its own claims.

flashcards.prompt: What did the six case studies actually demonstrate about Danus?
flashcards.back_html: That the fact-graph mechanism lets Danus construct long, detailed proofs across algebraic geometry, singularity theory, and combinatorics — a demonstration of proof-building capability, not a claim of resolving previously open research problems.
